paras: The whipping of Samuel Low and West Regan was an attack by seven disguised men on two Black men in the Duck River bottom of Humphreys County, Tennessee, on Friday, August 21, 1885. Low was given more than one hundred blows with ironwood switches, and Regan was beaten and driven from the county. Wire dispatches from Nashville presented the attack as one of a series of "Ku-Klux outrages" in the county, and the story was reprinted from New York to Minnesota and in the Black weekly Cleveland Gazette.

According to a Nashville dispatch of August 23, "a more or less bitter feeling" had existed for months between some white and Black residents of Humphreys County. The same dispatch reported that a Black man who had tried to escape a crowd intending to beat him was shot, and his body was found near his cabin the next morning. Other Black residents had been taken out and lashed, and no one had been arrested for any of these acts.

The band first seized West Regan, who was given twenty blows and ordered to leave the county, which he did at once. The men then went to Low's home, presented revolvers at him, and dragged him from his bed. They took him to the woods and beat him with ironwood switches, "lacerating his back in a horrible manner," leaving him seriously ill and unable to leave his bed for some days.

In the same neighborhood, John Gorin, a Black school teacher, found a note on his door warning him to leave the county or suffer the consequences. The dispatch said Gorin was "very much alarmed" and left immediately.

No arrests were reported. The Nashville dispatch stated that "the best citizens" of Humphreys County condemned the outrages and would likely ask the governor to offer a reward for the guilty parties. No report of a reward, an investigation or any later proceedings appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press in two Nashville dispatches: a short one dated August 22, run by the New York Sun as "Kn-Klux Outrages in Tennessee" and reprinted by the Washington Evening Star, and a fuller one dated August 23, carried by the St. Paul Daily Globe under "Whipping Negroes." The Hickman Courier in Kentucky printed the longer text as "A Race War in Tennessee." These white papers ran the dispatch without editorial comment, though its own wording, "brutally lashed" and "horrible manner," was critical of the attackers.

The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, reprinted the full dispatch on August 29 under the headline "Ku-Klux Outrages" with the deck "Peaceable Negroes Brutally Beaten and Forced to Leave Their Homes in Tennessee," stressing that the victims had done nothing to provoke the attack. In Iowa, the Republican Oskaloosa Herald used a version of the dispatch from the New York Times in a partisan editorial, calling it "a further sample of Democratic love for the colored man."
The wire texts give Regan twenty blows, while the Oskaloosa Herald's paraphrase says "twenty-three lashes"; the names also appear as "Lowe" and "Reagan" in some reprints.

accounts.label: Nashville wire dispatch, Aug. 22 (short)
accounts.gist: Masked men took Low from his cabin and gave him over 100 lashes, gave Regan twenty and ordered him out, warned Gorin; a Black man who fled a beating had been shot dead; no arrests.

accounts.label: Nashville wire dispatch, Aug. 23 (full)
accounts.gist: Places the attack in months of bitter feeling between white and Black citizens; seven disguised men with revolvers seized Regan and then Low; best citizens condemn and may seek a reward.

framing.detail: The Sun ran the short dispatch as 'Kn-Klux Outrages in Tennessee', and the Globe ran the full one as 'Whipping Negroes', both without comment.
The Oskaloosa Herald cited the dispatch as 'a further sample of Democratic love for the colored man' in a partisan editorial.
The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the full dispatch under 'Ku-Klux Outrages' with a deck calling the victims 'Peaceable Negroes Brutally Beaten'.

conflicts.note: The Iowa editorial's figure is a secondhand paraphrase; the wire texts all say twenty.
Spelling variants of the same persons; the Hickman Courier also prints 'Lowe' and 'Reagan'.
